overview:
On a clear Tuesday morning, nineteen men associated with al-Qaeda boarded four transcontinental flights leaving Boston, Newark and Washington Dulles, chosen because they were heavily fueled for the run to California. Armed with box cutters and small knives, they seized the cockpits within minutes of takeoff. American Airlines Flight 11 struck the north tower of the World Trade Center at 8:46 a.m.; United Airlines Flight 175 hit the south tower at 9:03, by which time television cameras were already trained on lower Manhattan and much of the world watched the second impact live. American Airlines Flight 77 was flown into the western face of the Pentagon at 9:37. On United Airlines Flight 93, delayed on the tarmac at Newark, passengers learned by cell and airphone what had happened in New York and rushed the cockpit; the aircraft went down in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:03, short of a target most investigators believe was the Capitol or the White House. The south tower collapsed at 9:59 and the north tower at 10:28, burying the surrounding blocks in pulverized concrete and burning jet fuel; the 47-story World Trade Center 7, unhit but on fire and unfought, came down that afternoon. In all, 2,977 people were killed, from some ninety countries, including several hundred firefighters and police who had climbed into the towers as others descended.

The plot came out of a movement shaped by the anti-Soviet war in Afghanistan. Osama bin Laden had built al-Qaeda from that milieu and by 1998 was publicly calling for the killing of Americans anywhere; the network had already bombed two U.S. embassies in East Africa and the destroyer USS Cole. The specific idea of turning airliners into weapons was pitched to bin Laden by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed in the late 1990s, and the operation was staffed partly from a cell of educated expatriates in Hamburg, one of whom, Mohamed Atta, became its tactical leader. American intelligence agencies had fragments of this — two of the future hijackers were known to the CIA and not watchlisted, an FBI field office had flagged suspicious flight-school students — but the pieces never combined into warning. The 9/11 Commission, reporting in 2004, called it a failure of imagination as much as of capability.

The response was immediate and enormous. American airspace was cleared, then rebuilt around new screening rules; within a month the United States and allies were at war in Afghanistan against the Taliban government that had sheltered bin Laden. Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act in October 2001 and created the Department of Homeland Security the next year. The Bush administration's broader "war on terror" produced the detention camp at Guantánamo Bay, a CIA program of secret prisons and coercive interrogation, and in 2003 the invasion of Iraq, justified in part by claims about weapons and terrorism that did not hold up. Bin Laden was killed by U.S. forces in Pakistan in 2011. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, captured in 2003, has still not been tried; the military commission case against him remains unresolved more than two decades on, snarled largely by the legal consequences of how he was interrogated.
significance: Few single days have redirected so much at once. The attacks ended a decade in which the United States had faced no serious external threat and inaugurated two long wars, a permanent architecture of surveillance and border control, and a set of legal improvisations — indefinite detention, extraordinary rendition, torture euphemistically renamed — whose costs are still being argued over in American courts and politics. Abroad, the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq reshaped the politics of Central and Southwest Asia for a generation and left states whose instability outlived the occupations. The everyday texture of travel, of policing, of what a government may know about its citizens, changed in most of the world and has not changed back. And the images themselves — two towers, a clear sky — became one of the small number of visual events that people across the planet can date precisely from memory.
coverage: Written from the 9/11 Commission's executive summary, the National September 11 Memorial's published figures, and NIST's engineering investigations; the dataset holds only the five events of the morning itself — the four flights and the towers' collapse — and nothing of the wars, legislation, or long health aftermath described here. The minute-by-minute record of that day is exceptionally well documented, but the account of how the plot was conceived rests heavily on interrogations of detainees held in CIA custody and subjected to coercive methods, material the Commission itself could not question its sources about directly; that portion of the story should be read as the best available reconstruction rather than settled testimony. Long-term deaths from World Trade Center dust exposure now number in the thousands and are still accumulating, and roughly a thousand victims' remains have never been identified.
